title: Italy’s expanded first-home guarantee brought additional young borrowers into the mortgage market
summary: A Banca d’Italia study finds that the 2021 expansion of Italy’s First-Home Guarantee Fund, combined with tax incentives, increased new mortgage lending to young borrowers by about 36% relative to other borrowers. The authors estimate €13.3bn of additional credit from July 2021 to December 2023. That is roughly three-quarters of the guaranteed credit in their calculation. The remainder illustrates why the face value of guaranteed mortgages is a poor measure of credit creation. Some borrowers would have obtained a mortgage even without the package. The paper evaluates originations. It does not estimate the number of additional homeowners, the eventual default bill or the return earned by the government (pp. 5–6, 19–24).

The original fund backed up to half the principal on eligible mortgages up to €250,000. The enhanced scheme offered up to 80% coverage for qualifying younger borrowers, including under-36s whose means-tested ISEE indicator did not exceed €40,000, on mortgages above 80% of the property purchase price. Those borrowers could obtain loans financing up to the entire price. The guarantee limits the lender’s exposure to principal loss. A high loan-to-value mortgage separately reduces the cash the household must put down and leaves it with less initial equity. Purchase-tax relief and the restrictions on loan pricing also affected affordability. These features changed together. Interpreting the estimate as the effect of an 80% guarantee in isolation would overstate the evidence (Section 3 and Appendix A).

The researchers assembled a 2011–23 sample of around 4.3 million mortgage contracts using the Italian Central Credit Register. More than 330,000 carried a fund guarantee, and a matched survey supplied loan rates for a subset. They examined local credit flows, used differences in banks’ propensity to originate guaranteed loans across local markets, and compared lending to younger and older borrowers before and after the reform. The methods address different sources of selection. A bank that already served younger customers or operates where demand is rising might otherwise appear particularly successful simply because it originated more qualifying loans. The age-group comparison relies on the groups having followed similar paths in the absence of the reform. Appendix D shows the pre-treatment estimates around that comparison (Sections 4–6, Tables 2–6).

The stronger results concern the enhanced package introduced in 2021. The earlier 50% guarantee yielded much less convincing evidence of additional credit. The local estimates also varied systematically with economic conditions. The authors grouped labour markets using income, employment and labour-force participation measured before the original fund existed. The increase in lending was larger in more disadvantaged locations. Figure 7 breaks these estimates down further by local house-price levels and shows the uncertainty around them. A lower down payment can make the largest difference where young households have least financial wealth. The estimates do not identify the constraint faced by each borrower.

For a lender, larger origination volumes and lower loss exposure on guaranteed balances may both matter. For a household, more access to credit comes with a larger debt relative to its own equity. Neither implication establishes a lasting increase in ownership if scarce housing supply instead drives up sale prices. The paper identifies homeownership outcomes, interactions with regional housing programmes, the distribution of benefits to lenders and the fiscal cost as open questions. These are necessary inputs to a comparison between marginal lending and the guarantees ultimately called (pp. 21–24).

questions.question: Did additional mortgages translate into first-time ownership that persisted?
questions.detail: The paper estimates additional credit flows, while moving the timing of an already planned purchase could also raise observed originations. Match title registrations, subsequent sales and household tenure histories by age and location, accounting for tax-relief dates and regional programmes. This would distinguish a lasting expansion in the borrower base from a temporary concentration of demand and help assess future mortgage volumes.

questions.question: How does the risk of the additional loan book compare with the government’s contingent liability?
questions.detail: A guarantee shifts part of a principal loss to the state, while high loan-to-value borrowing leaves little borrower equity at entry. The study does not follow foreclosures to final recovery. Compare origination cohorts’ arrears, refinancing, defaults, collateral recoveries and guarantees called in Consap and credit-register records, conditioning on leverage and rates. Both bank loss severity and the fiscal value of the programme depend on that sequence.

questions.question: Did tight local housing supply absorb the benefit through higher prices?
questions.detail: The larger lending effects occurred in economically weaker areas, but the analysis does not establish who captured the subsidy. Compare achieved prices, completed purchases and construction permits in local markets with different development constraints and exposure to participating banks. Price capitalisation would have different implications for existing collateral and affordability than new supply meeting young buyers’ demand.
